question.text: Do inhaled corticosteroids affect perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction in asthma?
question.context: Some of the disagreements on the perception of dyspnea (PD) during bronchoconstriction in asthma patients could depend on the interrelationships among the following: (1) the influence of baseline airflow obstruction on the patient's ability to detect any further increase in airway resistance; (2) the effect of eosinophilic inflammation on the airway; (3) bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR); and (4) the effect of inhaled corticosteroids (ICSs). We hypothesized that if the inflammation of the airway wall influences to some extent and in some way the PD in asthma patients, ICSs reverse the effect of airway inflammation on the PD. We studied 100 asthma patients who were divided into the following four groups: patients with obstruction who were either ICS-naive (group I) or were treated with ICSs (group II); and nonobstructed patients who were either ICS-naive (group III) or were treated with ICSs (group IV). PD on the visual analog scale (VAS) was assessed during a methacholine-induced FEV(1) decrease and specifically was quantified as the VAS slope and score at an FEV(1) decrease of 5 to 20%. BHR was assessed in terms of the provocative concentration of methacholine causing a 20% fall in FEV(1) (PC(20)). Eosinophil counts in induced sputum samples also were performed. Regression analysis, univariate analysis of variance, and factor analysis were applied for statistical evaluation. For a 5 to 20% fall in FEV(1) from the lowest point after saline solution induction, VAS score was lowest in group II, slightly higher in group I, slightly higher still in group IV, and the highest in group III. In the patients as a whole, BHR related to PD, but age, clinical score, duration of the disease, and presence of baseline airway obstruction did not. In patients with obstruction who were treated with ICSs, eosinophil counts related to PD negatively. Factor analysis yielded the following four factors that accounted for 70% of the variance in the data: ICS; eosinophil counts; FEV(1); and PC(20) loaded on separated factors with PD loading on the same factors as PC(20). The post hoc analysis carried out dividing the patients into ICS-treated and ICS-naive, showed that in the former group eosinophil counts and BHR proved to be factors negatively associated with PD, while in the latter group eosinophil counts were positively associated with PD.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that ICS treatment was associated with a *decrease* in perceived dyspnea (PD) in asthma patients, particularly in those with airway obstruction. This suggests that ICSs can reduce the perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction. The study also showed that eosinophil counts and BHR were negatively associated with PD in ICS-treated patients, further supporting the idea that ICSs can alleviate the perception of dyspnea.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The study found that in the patients as a whole, BHR related to PD, but age, clinical score, duration of the disease, and presence of baseline airway obstruction did not. In patients with obstruction who were treated with ICSs, eosinophil counts related to PD negatively.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could influence PD, the study's findings strongly suggest that ICSs have a direct effect on reducing the perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction in asthma. Other factors like age, clinical score, duration of the disease, and presence of baseline airway obstruction were not significant predictors of PD, making the effect of ICSs more prominent.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that inhaled corticosteroids (ICSs) reduce dyspnea perception during bronchoconstriction in asthma patients. Group II (ICS-treated obstructive patients) showed the lowest VAS score during methacholine challenge, indicating reduced dyspnea perception. The post hoc analysis revealed that ICS-treated patients had negative associations between eosinophil counts and BHR with PD, suggesting ICSs mitigate the effect of inflammation on dyspnea perception.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: In ICS-treated patients, eosinophil counts and BHR were negatively associated with PD, showing ICSs reverse the effect of airway inflammation on dyspnea perception.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed - this is a straightforward pharmacological study evaluating the effect of ICSs on dyspnea perception, not a diagnostic case.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows that ICS-treated patients (group II) had the lowest VAS scores during bronchoconstriction, indicating reduced perception of dyspnea, and eosinophil counts negatively correlated with PD in this group. This suggests ICSs modulate the relationship between airway inflammation and dyspnea perception. The post hoc analysis further confirms that ICS treatment reverses the positive association between eosinophils and PD seen in ICS-naive patients.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: In ICS-treated patients, eosinophil counts negatively associated with PD, while in ICS-naive patients, eosinophil counts positively associated with PD — indicating ICSs alter the inflammatory-perception relationship.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Differential considerations included whether baseline obstruction or BHR alone explained PD — but the study found BHR related to PD overall, while ICS treatment independently modulated PD perception, especially in obstructed patients, ruling out obstruction as the sole factor.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The key finding is that in ICS-treated asthma patients (group II), both eosinophil counts and BHR are negatively associated with perceived dyspnea (PD), indicating that inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness, which are reduced by ICS, are linked to lower perception of dyspnea. In contrast, ICS-naive patients with obstruction (group I) show the opposite association. This suggests that inhaled corticosteroids reduce the underlying inflammation and hyperresponsiveness that otherwise increase the perception of dyspnea, supporting the idea that inhaled corticosteroids do affect perception of dyspnea during bronchoconstriction in asthma patients.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: In the ICS-treated group, eosinophil counts and BHR are negatively associated with PD, meaning lower inflammation and lower BHR are linked to lower perceived dyspnea.
